## Introduction 

This write-up describes how the metric Deprivation gap in early cancer diagnosis
is derived for the NHS Oversight Framework.

[NHS England » NHS Oversight Framework 2026/27](https://www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/nhs-oversight-framework-2026-27/)

### Definitions

To make sure we're all on the same page, here's some working definitions for
what we're talking about.

**Early cancer diagnosis** 

The proportion of cancers diagnosed at stage 1 and 2 out of all cancers
diagnosed at stages 1 to 4, observed over a 12-month period.

**Deprivation**

Uses Index of Multiple Deprivation (IMD) quintiles from 1 to 5, representing the
most deprived to least deprived areas in groups of 20%. These quintiles are
derived nationally, which makes it possible to compare across geographies, but
may mean some groups are over/under-represented in different areas.

**Deprivation Gap**

The difference in early diagnosis proportion between those in the most and least
deprived groups. That is, a measure of the relationship between deprivation and
the early diagnosis of cancer.

**Slope Index of Inequality (SII)** 

An SII is an absolute measure of inequality that represents the difference in
predicted values of an indicator between the most advantaged and most
disadvantaged subgroups, obtained by fitting a regression model, or line of best
fit. It is a standard method of measuring inequality in public health, used by
both Public Health England (PHE) and the World Health Organisation (WHO).

PHE: 
[Technical Guidance - Slope Index of Inequality](https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/static-reports/public-health-technical-guidance/Inequality/SII.html)

WHO Health Inequalities Handbook:
[Summary measures based on ordered inequality dimensions](https://whoequity.github.io/book_2024/4_analysis-reporting/Chapter21.html)

### Why use a Slope Index of Inequality

The Slope Index of Inequality (SII) was selected because it provides a robust and well-established measure of the relationship between deprivation and early cancer diagnosis. At the all-cancer level there is a strong linear relationship between deprivation quintile and the proportion of cancers diagnosed at an early stage, making a regression-based approach appropriate.

A key advantage of the SII is that it uses data from all deprivation quintiles rather than relying solely on the most and least deprived groups. This is particularly important at ICB level, where some quintiles may contain relatively small numbers of cases. Simpler measures, such as the change in the least deprived quintile over time or the difference between quintiles 5 and 1, can be more sensitive to random variation and are therefore less robust.

The SII is also a widely recognised measure of health inequality. It is routinely used by the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities (OHID) and is recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) for measuring and comparing inequalities across population groups.


## How we measure the gap

We'll start with an example representing national early diagnosis by
deprivation.

```{r class.source="fold-hide"}

example_df <- data.frame(
  deprivation = c("1 - most deprived", "2", "3", "4", "5 - least deprived"),
  ed_prop = c(0.555, 0.58, 0.595, 0.606, 0.619),
  ed_denom = c(39546, 43663, 48796, 51117, 50739)
)

example_df |> 
  transform(ed_prop = paste0(ed_prop * 100, "%")) |> 
  knitr::kable()
```

Visually, with the number of cases as the size of the points:

```{r class.source = NULL}

example_df |> 
  ggplot() + 
  aes(y = ed_prop, x = deprivation) +
  geom_point(aes(size = ed_denom)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0.55, .65)) +
  scale_size_continuous(limits = c(0, 55000), range = c(10, 12)) +
  labs(title = "Early Diagnosis Proportion by Deprivation",
       x = "Deprivation Quintile",
       y = "Early Diagnosis Proportion (%)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")  
```

### Quintile 5 minus Quintile 1

As a point of reference, a simple and direct way to measure the distance between
the extremes would be to just take the difference between the early stage
proportion in quintiles 1 and 5.

$$
61.9\text{%} - 55.0\text{%} = 6.9 \text{pp}
$$

Note we measure this as a percentage point (pp) for a difference between
percentages. So we could say the least deprived quintile has 6.9 percentage
point higher chance of being diagnoses at an early stage than the most deprived
quintile.


### Building a line of best 

The SII expands on this by including all deprivation quintiles and fitting a
linear regression model across them. For this purpose we scale the deprivation
quintile groups between 0 and 1. Each quintile is assigned to the midpoint of
the proportion of the population it represents. For example, the first 20%,
quintile 1, is placed at 0.1 (or 10%). This has the neat benefit that the
regression model gradient represents the change in early diagnosis proportion
across the whole deprivation range, instead of the change for a 1 unit increase
in deprivation quintile. With this we can take the gradient directly as the
value of the SII. This is equivalent to taking the difference between the
modelled early diagnosis proportion at 0 and 1 on the scaled axis, which tends
to give a larger gap than subtracting quintile 1 from quintile 5 (which would
sit at 0.1 and 0.9 on our scale).

```{r class.source = "fold-show"}

example_df |> 
  ggplot() + 
  aes(y = ed_prop, x = c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = ed_denom)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", 
              formula = y ~ x,
              se = FALSE, 
              fullrange = TRUE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0.55, .65)) +
  scale_size_continuous(limits = c(0, 55000), range = c(10, 12)) +
  labs(title = "Early Diagnosis Proportion by Deprivation",
       x = "Scaled Deprivation Quintile",
       y = "Early Diagnosis Proportion (%)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    breaks = c(0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1),
    expand = c(0, 0)
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")  
```

### Adding weighting


Given that we are using nationall derived IMD quintiles, using even spacing /
weighting will not hold when we look at different organisations, which will have
a highly variable number of cases in different quintiles. So, when fitting the
regression line, not all deprivation quintiles provide the same amount of
information. A quintile based on 1,500 staged cancers gives us a more precise
estimate of the early diagnosis proportion than a quintile based on only 300
cancers.

To account for this, we use weighted least squares regression. Each deprivation
quintile is assigned a weight based on the inverse variance of a binomial
proportion:

$$
w_i = \frac{n_i}{p_i(1-p_i)}
$$

where:

* \(n_i\) is the number of staged cancers in deprivation group \(i\)
* \(p_i\) is the early diagnosis proportion in deprivation group \(i\)
* \(w_i\) is the weight applied in the regression

This weighting reflects the statistical precision of each observed proportion.
Larger groups receive more weight because they contain more information, while
proportions close to 50% receive slightly less weight than proportions near 0%
or 100%, as binomial variance is greatest when \(p = 0.5\).

Consider two fictional ICBs:

```{r}
icb_example <- tibble::tribble(
  ~icb, ~deprivation,       ~ed_prop, ~ed_denom,
  "A", "1 - most deprived",  0.552,   500,
  "A", "2",                  0.595,   700,
  "A", "3",                  0.580,   800,
  "A", "4",                  0.595,   1200,
  "A", "5 - least deprived", 0.607,   1500,
  "B", "1 - most deprived",  0.585,   900,
  "B", "2",                  0.594,   800,
  "B", "3",                  0.552,   1000,
  "B", "4",                  0.591,   800,
  "B", "5 - least deprived", 0.615,   700,
)
```

We'll fit the SII for each using our package function:

```{r}
icb_example <- icb_example |> 
  derive_sii(
    by = "icb", 
    ed_prop_col = "ed_prop",
    ed_denom_col = "ed_denom",
    depr_col = "deprivation"
  )
```

Then use a helper function to visualise the fit for each organisation:

```{r}
icb_example <- plot_sii(icb_example, id = "icb")
```

Looking at ICB A we can see the linear model working fairly well, but also see
that more precise points are favoured. The line is much closer to the quintiles
with more cases than especially the first quintile with less.

```{r}
icb_example$plot[[1]]
```

ICB B has more variability between quintiles, with a smaller deprivation gap,
but a poorer fitting model as the relationship is less clearly linear.

```{r}
icb_example$plot[[2]]
```

## Oversight Framework Scoring

The 1-4 scoring for the cancer early diagnosis (ED) deprivation gap, is as
defined in the table below. This shows that ICB scoring is based on both the
difference from the England average and the size of the statistical variation
(standard deviation) associated with this gap. The statistical variation here
measures how close a correlation there is between ED and deprivation, and
whether this is based on a larger or smaller number or patients. For example,
it’s possible that an ICB with a smaller deprivation gap but more statistical
variation may score lower than an ICB with a larger gap but less variation.

| SII score | Description |
|:--|:-------- |
| 1 | Strong evidence for a smaller-than-average deprivation gap: More than 2 Standard Errors below the England average. |
| 2 | Some evidence for a smaller-than-average deprivation gap: 1-2 Standard Errors below the England average |
| 3 | No evidence for a smaller-than-average deprivation gap: 1 Standard Error below to 1 Standard Error above the England average |
| 4 | Evidence for a larger-than-average deprivation gap: More than 1 Standard Error above the England average |

With our example ICBs we showed the SII and also the standard error of the SII. If we had a mean of 9 percentage points gap 
across all ICBs in England, and compare that back this to our outputs:

```{r}
icb_example |> 
  subset(select = c("icb", "sii", "sii_std_err")) |> 
  transform(sii = paste0(round(sii, 4) * 100, " p.p."),
            sii_std_err = paste0(round(sii_std_err, 4) * 100, " p.p.")) |> 
  knitr::kable()  
```

We can see that ICB A would fall into group 1, because 
$9 - 2 \times 1.92 = 5.16$, and $5.06$ is less than that. ICB B would score in 
group _2_ because $9 - 2 \times 4.07 = 0.86$, and $9 - 4.07 = 4.93$, where 
$2.53$ falls in that 1 to 2 standard errors range. Thus an organisation with a
lower deprivation gap might not score as well, because there is less confidence
in the fit of the model.

## Applying this package across all organisations

First some dummy data, an org with random values
for each letter of the alphabet in `icb_dummy_data`. 

```{r}
glimpse(NHSOFearlystagecancer::icb_dummy_data)
```

We can get the SII and score for each of them, with a simple pipeline, as long as we correctly specify the groups with the `by` argument:

```{r}
icb_results <- NHSOFearlystagecancer::icb_dummy_data |>
  derive_sii(
    by = c("date", "org_code"),
    ed_prop_col = "ed_prop",
    ed_denom_col = "ed_denom",
    depr_col = "deprivation"
  ) |>
  score_sii(by = "date") |> 
  plot_sii(id = "org_code")

icb_results |> 
  select(date, org_code, sii, sii_std_err, sii, sii_mean, sii_score)
```

With a plot for each organisation:

```{r}
icb_results |> 
  filter(org_code == "X") |> 
  pull(plot)
```
